This is the teacher's stricter usage. By the textbook definition, networked components that communicate and coordinate to do one job already form a distributed system; what the teacher means is that it is not a well-designed (scalable, fault-tolerant) one.
precise_version: Remote machines talking to each other are technically a distributed system, but not a good one unless every layer scales and tolerates failure.

note: Horizontal scale is one main reason to build distributed systems, but not the definition. Fault tolerance (no single failure takes the system down) and geographic distribution are equally common reasons; the board lists fault tolerance, and the teacher separates the two motives later (L-0288).
precise_version: Distributed systems are built to scale horizontally and to tolerate failures of individual machines.

Conflates scalability with availability. A layer that cannot scale out is a capacity bottleneck; it is a single point of failure only if it also has no redundancy. A single-writer database with a synchronous standby and automatic failover (RDS Multi-AZ) cannot scale out but is not a SPOF. The teacher's own example later is a single CoreDNS-style node with a standby. Conversely, a scaled-out tier behind a single load balancer still has a SPOF.
precise_version: A layer that cannot scale horizontally is a bottleneck; if it also has no standby or failover, it is a single point of failure.

note: Stated as absolute, but the teacher relaxes it (L-0044: a non-scalable database is fine if it handles the load) and later uses a single active node with a standby. The real requirement for every layer is enough capacity for peak load and no unprotected single point of failure; scaling out is one way to get that, a standby is another.

Google SRE recommends measuring capacity in resources (CPU) rather than queries per second.

True at the protocol level: TCP has no idle timeout, keep-alives are optional, off by default and at least 2 hours apart (RFC 9293). In practice, middleboxes on the path close idle connections: load balancers (AWS ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 s), NATs and firewalls. A learner designing an hour-long request must send data or keep-alives, or raise those timeouts; otherwise the connection is dropped silently.
precise_version: TCP itself never times out an idle connection, but load balancers, NATs and firewalls on the path do, so long-lived connections need keep-alives or periodic data.

note: Reversed default: since HTTP/1.1, connections are persistent by default, and a client or server must send 'Connection: close' to end one. Closing after each response was HTTP/1.0 behaviour, where the 'keep-alive' option kept the connection open. Persistence also does not by itself let one request run for an hour; idle timeouts on proxies still apply.
precise_version: HTTP/1.0 closed the connection after each response unless keep-alive was used; HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default.

note: gRPC does use long-lived HTTP/2 connections that the protocol does not time out (server MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE and MAX_CONNECTION_AGE default to infinite). But proxies and load balancers can treat them as idle and drop them, which is why gRPC has HTTP/2 PING keepalives. Servers can also be configured to close connections or send GOAWAY.

Two corrections. (1) Some common servers do give tooling: Go's net/http cancels the request Context 'when the client's connection closes', so a handler can stop work. (2) The socket only reports a disconnect when a FIN or RST arrives. A peer that vanished (power loss, cable cut, dropped NAT entry) goes unnoticed until you write or keep-alive probes fail, because TCP 'does not inherently include a liveness detection capability' (RFC 9293).
Both offer cancellation: Redshift's CANCEL command stops a running query; BigQuery can cancel a running job, though success is not guaranteed and charges may still apply.

Redis's lock guide describes exactly this edge case: a client blocked past the lock's TTL may delete a lock now held by another client, so plain DEL is unsafe and the release must be an atomic compare-and-delete.

The example just shown (Redlock across five Redis nodes) was made distributed for fault tolerance, not for horizontal scale; the teacher says so in L-0287. 'Horizontally scalable like this' blurs the two; the point is that no piece should be a single instance whose failure stalls the system.

Matches the Redis docs: Redlock's added property is fault tolerance ('as long as the majority of Redis nodes are up, clients are able to acquire and release locks'), at the cost of contacting N nodes per acquire. Replicating for availability generally costs write latency (e.g. RDS Multi-AZ synchronous replication).
Correct distinction. In practice one design often serves both purposes (read replicas add capacity and redundancy), but the motives are different.
